title: NASA’s Swift Telescope Ends Its Long Mission
paragraphs: After nearly 22 years of work, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has reached the end of its science mission. The telescope was built to study gamma-ray bursts, brief but enormously energetic flashes of light, and its combination of optical, ultraviolet and X-ray instruments allowed it to pinpoint a burst within moments of its detection. It launched on November 20, 2004, and was renamed in 2018 to honour its first principal investigator, Neil Gehrels, who had died.

The cause of the retirement is not a technical failure but physics. Swift’s orbit has decayed below 275 kilometres, where drag from the atmosphere is strong enough to prevent its telescopes from holding steady on a target. Its last observation was made on October 20, and the spacecraft is expected to re-enter the atmosphere within weeks. A mission designed to last two years therefore operated for more than ten times as long.

The scientific legacy is substantial: more than 2,000 bursts observed, more than 1,400 supernovae studied and roughly 7,000 published papers. In 2005 Swift detected the afterglow of a short burst for the first time, which supported the idea that such flashes come from merging neutron stars. Its principal investigator, S. Bradley Cenko, said Swift “was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts.” NASA says other missions will now fill the gap.

questions.a: Its orbit decayed and atmospheric drag stopped its telescopes from observing steadily.
It detected the afterglow of a short gamma-ray burst for the first time, supporting the neutron-star merger idea.

questions.q: Was the end caused by a technical failure?
questions.a: No, it was caused by the decaying orbit.
